title: Whether Columbia kept Bessie Smith masters
summary: Speculation on surviving Columbia masters, the company's many owners and how Brunswick and Decca rights confused reissues.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I understand that Columbia did not have the original presses of Bessie Smith. They had destroyed them all or thrown them away.

I think most of them had been, but I do think, though, when the Valkian went through their files that they did find some of them. I know they did find, like, the one at the Christmas ball. Were there two of those? Yeah, what was the other one? I can't think of the other one. So I think...
Unissued ones, is that what you did?

Yeah, so if they had some of the unissued ones there, they probably had some of the others there, too, I think. Although at one time, I know other opera collectors told me once, see, Columbia went bankrupt four or five times, I think, if that's possible, probably under different names, the American Record Corporation and all those. At one time, some of the stuff was sold out to Brunswick, and some of that stuff... When Steve Smith, I mentioned, started his record store called Hot Records Society, that was entirely his own project, and he also reissued records on the HRS, Hot Records Society, label. And... And... When he wanted to put out some of the old Brunswick material, an old Vicalion, Columbia didn't know whether they owned it, and some of it was owned by Decca. The Warner Brothers had bought some of it once from Columbia, or the Brunswick Corporation, or something. See, at one time, that was a company that made billiard.

Yeah. Worked in Bakelite, and the hard rubber, and all that kind of junk. So... Anyway, I imagine Columbia had quite a few of the Bessies there. As late as 1939 or so. But... Oh, I was going to say, this opera collector told me, once at one period, they knew that you could go up to Bridgeport and buy any original master that you wanted to, the metal plate, for $5 was the price they'd sell. including their early opera. They had some early 1900 or 19... from 1900 to 1905 period opera on a silver label, I think it was. No, it was a red label at first. That's right. Victor sued them, so they couldn't use the red label anymore. But they would have sold anything, including... that nobody in those days would have paid $5 to get a Bessie Smith or a King Oliver master, I don't think. But some of the opera collectors did go up and buy some of those things. That's what I'd heard. So, it would be a wonder if they had very many of their old masters there, but I imagine they did. Surprisingly, they saved those Bessies and a couple of the Louie's too, like Chicago Breakdown.
